what_its_for: Lidocaine is a local numbing medicine (anesthetic) that helps relieve pain by blocking nerve signals in a specific area of your body. Depending on the form, it can be used to numb skin before a needle stick or minor procedure, relieve pain from minor cuts, burns, or skin irritations, ease discomfort from mouth sores or sore throat, reduce pain from hemorrhoids or rectal irritation, or manage nerve pain (such as from shingles when used as a skin patch).
how_to_take: Lidocaine comes in many forms including creams, gels, ointments, sprays, patches, and injections given by a healthcare provider. Always use the exact form your doctor or pharmacist told you to use. For creams, gels, or ointments: Clean and dry the affected area, then apply a thin layer directly to the skin or inside the mouth as directed. For patches: Remove the patch from its wrapper, peel off the backing, and apply the sticky side to the most painful area of skin. Do not apply to broken, irritated, or infected skin unless your doctor says it is okay. Wash your hands before and after applying any form of lidocaine.
dosing: Your dose depends on the form of lidocaine you are using and what it is being used for. Follow your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions exactly. For skin patches (like Lidoderm): Apply up to 3 patches at one time to intact skin for up to 12 hours within a 24-hour period, then remove for at least 12 hours. For topical creams or gels: Use only the amount directed, usually a thin layer applied 1 to 3 times daily. For mouth gels or rinses: Use only the small amount recommended by your doctor. Do not use more than directed, as too much lidocaine can be absorbed into your body and cause serious side effects.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose or application, apply it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed one and continue with your regular schedule. Do not use a double amount to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store lidocaine at room temperature, away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Used patches still contain medicine and must be folded sticky side together before throwing away safely in the trash, away from children and pets. Do not flush patches down the toilet. Do not freeze any form of lidocaine unless the label says it is okay.
what_to_avoid: Do not apply lidocaine to your eyes, inside your nose, or near your ears unless specifically told to do so by your doctor. Avoid applying to broken, infected, or severely irritated skin unless directed. Do not cover the treated area with tight bandages or plastic wrap unless your doctor instructs you to, as this can increase how much medicine is absorbed into your body. Avoid using heat sources such as heating pads, electric blankets, or heat lamps over a lidocaine patch, as heat increases absorption and the risk of side effects. Do not swallow lidocaine gel or solution unless it is specifically made to be swallowed. Avoid using more than directed.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you notice any of the following: dizziness, drowsiness, or confusion; blurred or double vision; ringing in the ears; numbness or tingling in areas other than where you applied the medicine; irregular or fast heartbeat; difficulty breathing or swallowing; seizures; severe allergic reaction such as hives, rash, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; or if the treated area becomes more red, swollen, or painful. Also call your doctor if your pain does not get better or gets worse.
when_it_works: Lidocaine works quickly, usually within a few minutes of application. Skin creams and gels typically start numbing the area within 2 to 5 minutes. Lidocaine patches may take 30 minutes to a few hours to provide the most pain relief. The numbing effect usually lasts 1 to 3 hours after you stop applying it, but this can vary.
special_populations: Children: Lidocaine should be used with great caution in infants and young children. Never use adult-strength numbing creams on babies or young children without a doctor's specific instructions. Too much lidocaine in small children can cause serious side effects. Pregnant women: Talk to your doctor before using lidocaine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding mothers: Small amounts of lidocaine may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before using if you are breastfeeding. Older adults: Elderly patients may be more sensitive to the effects of lidocaine. Use the lowest effective amount. Liver disease: If you have liver problems, lidocaine may build up in your body more than normal. Let your doctor know before using this medicine.
